disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating accompanied by a sense of loss of control, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, fasting, excessive exercise, or misuse of laxatives to prevent weight gain. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight, but individuals typically maintain a body weight within or near the normal range, distinguishing it from classic anorexia nervosa. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress, interpersonal difficulties, and body-image concerns. It is differentiated from binge-eating disorder by the regular use of compensatory behaviors and from normal overeating by the degree of loss of control and distress associated with the eating episodes.

narrative.personality: Julio is a sensitive, imaginative, and conscientious young man who pours himself into making others feel understood while quietly second-guessing his own worth.
narrative.stressor: Julio’s difficulties began after his tech support center shifted to stricter performance metrics, tying his job security and bonuses to call times, satisfaction scores, and sales targets. He started working frequent overtime, skipping regular meals during shifts and then coming home exhausted, feeling guilty about minor customer complaints and comparing himself harshly to thinner, more polished colleagues in marketing whose social media presence he admired. Food gradually became his main comfort and reward after stressful days, and he began planning solitary late-night takeout and grocery runs as an escape from the pressure and from feeling like he was falling behind his creative ambitions. Over several months, his eating patterns around these episodes grew more extreme and secretive, left him feeling ashamed about his body, and began to interfere with his energy for yoga, drawing, and socializing, prompting him to seek psychiatric help when he realized he no longer felt in control of how he was eating after work.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started eating way more than I mean to in one sitting, especially at night after work, and it feels like it’s getting out of hand.

narrative.personality: Alec is a calm, creatively inclined organizer who prefers flexibility over structure and often drifts into artistic projects and late-night routines despite good intentions to stay balanced.
narrative.stressor: Alec’s eating problems emerged in the context of a subtle but significant life transition when their office went fully hybrid and many long-time colleagues left or shifted roles, leaving them with a quieter workplace and looser boundaries between home and work. Without the old routine of shared lunches, commuting, and evening activities outside the house, they started staying up later, snacking while working on painting or puzzles, and using food to punctuate the long, unstructured evenings. At the same time, turning 40 had made them more self-conscious about aging, appearance, and the weight they had gradually gained, especially as they and their spouse began talking about long-term health and retirement plans. Over a few months, this mix of isolation, unstructured time, and mounting dissatisfaction with their body led to episodes of eating much more than intended during solitary nights, followed by intense regret and repeated attempts to “make up for it,” and they finally sought psychiatric care when these cycles began overshadowing their enjoyment of creative work and time with their spouse.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I find myself eating huge amounts late at night at home, way more than feels normal, and I can’t seem to rein it in.

narrative.personality: Lori is a warm, socially engaged planner who channels her anxiety into meticulous organizing of meaningful cultural and community experiences.
narrative.stressor: Lori’s current difficulties began after her adult children moved out of state within a short span of time, leaving her and her spouse adjusting to a quieter home and renegotiated roles after decades of parenting and community organizing. With more unstructured time and fewer daily caretaking tasks, she became increasingly preoccupied with how she looked and aged, especially when reconnecting with old acquaintances at arts events or seeing photos of herself alongside younger participants in her intergenerational programs. She began comparing her body harshly to both younger women and to her own image from earlier years, tying her sense of competence and attractiveness as a community leader to how slim and polished she appeared at events. Over several months, this growing focus on weight and shape drove more rigid and then chaotic eating and exercise habits behind the scenes, and when she noticed that her mood and self-worth were swinging dramatically based on the scale and how her clothes fit, she sought psychiatric help at the urging of a close friend from her book club who was worried about how consumed she had become with her appearance.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like how much I weigh and how my body looks has started to completely dictate how I feel about myself, and it’s really wearing me down.
